sentences.text: Jeholopterus is a small anurognathid pterosaur from the Daohugou Beds of northeast China, preserved with skin and feather-like structures.
The fossil preserves exquisite carbonized skin fibers and pycnofibres, revealing three layers of wing fibers that allowed the animal to adapt its wing profile.
It possessed relatively elongated wings with a wingspan of ninety centimeters.
The genus Jeholopterus was named in 2002 by Wang Xiaolin, Zhou Zhonghe, and Xu Xing.
The genus name Jeholopterus combines the place of discovery, Jehol, with the Greek word for wing.
The species name ningchengensis refers to Ningcheng County.
The paleoartist David Peters popularized unique interpretations of Jeholopterus without ever personally examining the fossil.

In 2003, David Peters claimed to have discovered soft tissue remains, including a horse-like tail used as a flyswatter or distractor, using image manipulation software, a finding disputed by other researchers.

David Peters suggested that Jeholopterus was a vampire-like pterosaur with rattlesnake fangs and a reinforced palate adapted to pierce tough skin, though this methodology has been strongly criticized.
Peters hypothesized that the small lower jaw teeth could not penetrate skin but could compress wounds like pincers.
Expert pterosaur researcher Chris Bennett described Peters' findings as a fantasy and vehemently denounced his methodology.
Researchers hypothesized that Jeholopterus might have been a piscivore because it was the largest known anurognathid.
Jeholopterus had mostly small, peg-like teeth, though some were longer and recurved.
Jeholopterus had a short neck with seven or eight cervical vertebrae.
Jeholopterus had robust wing bones and very short metacarpals.
Jeholopterus had a short pteroid bone that supported a propatagium pointing toward the body.
Jeholopterus possessed long, curved claws on its hands.
Jeholopterus had short but robust legs.
The elongated fifth toe suggests the presence of a membrane between the legs, the uropatagium.
It is debated whether the preserved wing tissue attached to the legs.
According to Wang et al., evidence suggests Jeholopterus's wings attached to the ankle.
Jeholopterus is classified within the family Anurognathidae.
Jeholopterus belongs to the parent group Anurognathidae.
The family of Jeholopterus is Anurognathidae.
Jeholopterus is classified within the class Reptilia.
Jeholopterus lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic in Inner Mongolia, China, and possibly the Early Cretaceous in North Korea.
Jeholopterus lived during the Callovian stage, between 165.3 and 161.5 million years ago.
There is one recorded fossil occurrence of Jeholopterus in the Paleobiology Database.
